DONATE TODAY Pope Leo calls for end to violence against West Bank Palestinian civilians August 16, 2026 At the conclusion of today’s Angelus address , Pope Leo XIV appealed for an end to violence against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank. “I renew my appeal for an end to the ongoing violence against the Palestinian civilian population in the West Bank,” Pope Leo said, to the applause of pilgrims in Castel Gandolfo ( video , 11:15), “and I urgently call on the international community to work toward advancing the two-state solution, for a just and lasting peace.” The Pontiff made his appeal as Christians in the West Bank face increasing intimidation from Israeli settlers. The Pope also recalled the Mediterranean Games , which begin on August 21 in Taranto, Italy: They will include various countries from Africa, Asia and Europe that are part of the Mediterranean region. I hope this sporting event will be a sign of peace and friendship among the peoples of this region and the entire world. As he extended greetings to pilgrims, the Pontiff said that “in greeting the Polish pilgrims, I extend my blessing to the many women participating in the traditional pilgrimage to the Shrine of Piekary Śląskie, in Upper Silesia.” The Polish city of 54,000 is the site of a Marian shrine ; Vatican News subsequently published an article on the pilgrimage. https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-v.text: Ursula von der Leyen hasn’t won the hearts and minds of EU citizens — if they know her at all. In a POLITICO poll conducted by pollster Public First across three major EU countries, only about one in five German and Spanish respondents said the Commission president was doing a good job; in France, just 12% said the same. Nearly one in three respondents in Spain and France, and 45% in Germany, said von der Leyen was doing a bad job. The poor performance review in von der Leyen’s homeland was largely driven by people who said they’d vote for the far-right Alternative for Germany party, with more than half of those voters saying she was doing a “very bad” job. Advertisement Advertisement In France and Spain, far more people said they didn’t consider her performance either good or bad; rather, they either had no opinion one way or the other or had never even heard of her. More than one in five French respondents said they didn’t know who von der Leyen was, compared with 10% in Spain and just 5% in Germany. The polling landed just hours before von der Leyen is set to outline her vision of the future of the bloc in her annual State of the Union address . “Von der Leyen is up against the same anti-political sentiment that has unseated incumbents across the continent, and will have to work hard to convince Europeans that any EU agenda is going to address their widespread concerns about the cost of living,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First, POLITICO’s polling partner. The polling numbers also showed that few citizens will be following von der Leyen’s speech live. Across the three countries, around one in 10 said they’d follow the address closely, while about one in three said they’d follow it a little. German respondents were more likely to pay attention to the speech. In Spain and France, more than half reported that they either wouldn’t follow the address despite being aware of it, or had never heard of it. Advertisement Advertisement Those numbers are likely still overstating how much respondents truly know or care about the State of the Union address, as respondents also reported that they’d follow a fictional “European Convention of Authority.” Public First’s survey was conducted from September 13 to 15, surveying more than 2,000 adults each in France, Germany and Spain. Results were weighted by age, gender, region and education as well as by the 2024 vote in France to match each country’s demographic profile. The margin of error is ±2.2 points for Spain and Germany and ±2.1 points for France.

Photograph: Oliver Dixon Gardens ‘It’s transformed the village’: the volunteers greening up Britain’s train stations Exclusive: Five gardening teams shortlisted for Royal Horticultural Society’s new Railway Stations in Bloom award Helena Horton Sun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Every year since 1964, towns across the UK have bloomed with hanging baskets and brightly coloured flowerbeds planted by residents. They wield their trowels in aid of the Royal Horticultural Society’s Britain in Bloom competition, a coveted accolade for the 1,600 communities that enter each year. Now, the charity is launching a new award for railway stations to honour the volunteers who keep platforms planted with cheerful flowers and pretty shrubs. Five of the best have been shortlisted for the RHS Railway Stations in Bloom competition, marked for their beauty but also for how well they welcome wildlife and withstand changing climate conditions. The winner, announced this week, was the Cardross Community Organic Garden in Scotland. The RHS said: “The judges were especially impressed by how active the group was in including different members of the community in the station’s activities, from school children, Brownies to other volunteering and gardening groups”. But all of the railway gardens are impressive. View image in fullscreen Cardross community organic garden in Scotland. Photograph: RHS It has been an extremely hot and dry summer in Alresford, Essex, but the gardeners were prepared. Working hard to cut through asphalt to create flowerbeds, they have planted a “dry garden” inspired by the horticultural pioneer Beth Chatto, who died in 2018 . Also from Essex, she managed to grow plants in dry ground that had never been cultivated. “It’s transformed the centre of the village,” said the lead volunteer, Frank Belgrave. Ten years ago the station was described in the local paper as “rundown”. Now, the planting beds rival any at Chelsea flower show. View image in fullscreen The entrance to Alresford railway station. Photograph: Oliver Dixon Belgrave said residents were very pleased their station had received the spruce-up: “It’s wonderful. People sometimes stop by with plants and compost to help us, and we are very lucky to have some lovely volunteers as the garden requires constant maintenance. “We used to spend all our time watering. So we decided to seek advice and build a dry garden with drought-resistant plants.” At a windswept station on the west coast of Scotland, commuters may be surprised to find trees heaving with fruit and a thriving vegetable patch. But Jane Connolly, who heads the Cardross station volunteer group, has found a way to create such bounty. “Since March 2022, every bit of the station that can be changed, has been changed,” she said. “We do have harsh winters – we don’t take summer bedding plants as we don’t get enough out of them – we choose hardy shrubs. We put up windproofing on the shore side to protect the plants but in general we have had very few failures.” Connolly and her fellow volunteers filled the station with plants from their own gardens and visit most days to tend to them. View image in fullscreen A boat planter at Cardross station. Photograph: RHS Having a pretty, flower-filled rail station rather than a neglected one makes a huge difference to the village, she said: “Every time we are down there, somebody will come along and peruse it and say how grateful they are with what we have done. I notice stations now wherever I go, even if it’s a window box. People come to our station just to see our gardens.” Other shortlisted stations include Maghull in Merseyside, where the ticket office’s window boxes are full of pretty flowers and volunteers have planted a woodland. At Wylde Green in Birmingham, overgrown areas were cleared and replaced with pollinator-friendly plants, creating a “bee corridor”. The volunteers carry out an annual butterfly count and have seen numbers increasing. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Pollinator-friendly plants are a focus at Wylde Green in Birmingham. Photograph: RHS Keynsham station in Somerset on a hot day looks especially exotic because volunteers have filled it with a remarkable array of succulents, of all shapes and sizes. Like the Essex gardeners, they have selected plants that will withstand hot summers. The volunteers at the stations have spoken of how social the job is and many have made friends. It also gives commuters a chance to chat. Belgrave said: “It’s very rewarding. Lots of people come and chat, they talk about plants, it gives them a social thing.” He hopes to get funding for a community hub and coffee shop. “On the platform there is a very ancient station house, to the back of that there was an area which was neglected and used as a community rubbish dump. We have turned that into a garden. Now, we hope we can open a coffee shop on the site.” View image in fullscreen The volunteer gardeners at the back of the old Alresford station house. Photograph: Oliver Dixon In Cardross, the gardeners have become fast friends. Connolly said: “We garden together and there is always laughing and joking and there is often more joking than working! We go out socialising together now as well. It is a very social thing.” Wildlife has returned to Alresford station, according to Belgrave. “We have noticed incredible amounts of wildlife, bees particularly. Honeybees, solitary bees, butterflies. That has changed a lot, we have seen the return of hedgehogs, we have slowworms.” The gardeners hope their example will encourage others to get involved. Belgrave said: “There are lots of stations which aren’t in the scheme, so if people do get involved it would be really good. It would be nice to see more stations planted up.” Explore more on these topics Gardens Rail transport Britain in Bloom Wildlife news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light
